query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the grain boundary density in HEA protective coatings through controlled post‐deposition annealing increases the rapid diffusion of oxide-forming elements to the surface, leading to the formation of a continuous, protective tribolayer that improves wear resistance under high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited HEA coating with a complex, multi-phase or nanocrystalline microstructure and an inherent grain boundary density.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment (by varying temperature and dwell time) to systematically increase the coating’s grain boundary density.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under sliding or abrasive conditions at elevated temperatures (up to approximately 900 °C) and representative loads used in wear-resistant applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density, which provides fast-diffusion pathways for critical oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr, Al) to reach the surface.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced diffusion along the grain boundaries accelerates the oxidation process during wear, promoting the formation of a continuous, protective oxide (tribolayer) that passivates the surface and reduces material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings subjected to the annealing treatment will develop a more continuous and robust tribolayer and will exhibit lower wear rates compared to the as-deposited baseline.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA coating without any additional annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The expected improvement should hold under wear conditions up to ~900 °C and within operational load ranges. However, if the annealing treatment is too aggressive, excessive grain growth may occur, potentially negating the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal annealing conditions (temperature and dwell time) and the quantitative relationship between increased grain boundary density and tribolayer formation kinetics remain uncertain and require further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA protective coatings: one set as-deposited (baseline) and a second set subjected to controlled post-deposition annealing designed to increase grain boundary density. Perform sliding wear tests at temperatures up to 900 °C under identical load conditions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of tribolayer formation and continuity using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Measurement of wear rates (e.g., mass loss or wear coefficient)
Grain boundary density evaluation via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tribolayer continuity and wear resistance compared to the as-deposited baseline, or if no corresponding increase in grain boundary density is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A single target containing the principal elements, CuMoTaWV, was partially sintered at 1000 °C using SPS to lower the cost and time of target preparation, as shown in Figure 1 . The elemental maps from the cross section of the target in Figure 1 b showed a uniform distribution of all of the elemental phases. This suggests that in the DC sputter film from the single target, the plasma will evaporate all of the principal elements to the substrate. The EDS area analyses from the cross section of the target in Table 2 and Table S1 showed a uniform distribution of elements with slightly lower amounts of Cu and W.

Preparation of a single target of CuMoTaWV: (a) SPS and (b) SEM morphology of the cross section of the target and elemental mapping.

The XRD diffractogram of the CuMoTaWV RHEA film deposited on the 304 stainless-steel substrate is shown in Figure 2 , together with the simulated XRD diffractogram obtained from the DFT-optimized SQS. The as-deposited film showed the formation of a single-phase BCC solid solution with a strong (110) preferred orientation. The experimentally determined lattice parameter is 3.18 Å, which is in good agreement with the one for the DFT-optimized SQS

Microstructure

An optical image of the as-cast HEA is shown in Figure 1 a, while the cross-section optical images of both processed samples are shown in Figure 1 b–e. The as-cast HEA showed coarse grains with an average grain size of nearly 100 μm. In contrast, both the SFP samples show a highly refined stir zone, and the grain size could not be obtained from the optical images. The depth of refinement (DOR) varies from 300 to 650 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively. The increment in DOR with rotational speed is likely due to the thick column of plastically deformed zone during processing at higher rotation speed. The grains of processed samples below the refined zone appear to be elongated, which is caused by the effect of shearing action and corresponds to the thermomechanical affected zone (TMAZ). Figure S1 shows the temperature profile acquired during the SFP at two different rotational speeds. At 400 rpm, the average temperature was nearly ∼280 °C, while it increased up to ∼760 °C at 1800 rpm. High temperature at higher rotational speed favors the material flow through thermal softening and leads to deeper DOR.

frame.system: High-entropy-alloy (HEA) protective coatings used in wear‐resistant applications, typically starting from as‐deposited coatings with complex, multi-phase or nanocrystalline microstructures.
frame.goal: To pinpoint a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the dominant control of wear performance in these HEA coatings and the origin of that control.
frame.limitation: There is an ambiguity in the field regarding which specific mechanism (e.g., tribolayer formation, dynamic recrystallization, oxidation-driven passivation, or grain boundary stabilization) primarily governs wear performance in HEAs. Previous studies have indicated several contributing factors but failed to decisively isolate one mechanism.
constraints: The hypothesis must be testable via a controlled change relative to a baseline state.
It should define a clear controlled parameter (e.g., microstructural state via heat treatment or compositional tuning) that is altered.
Directional observations (improved or degraded wear resistance based on the induced change) must be predicted if the hypothesis holds.
The hypothesis needs to specify the range (e.g., a range of applied loads or temperatures) over which it is expected to be valid.
Prior evidence supporting the hypothesis must be referenced, alongside an observation that would falsify it.
frame.regime: Wear testing under controlled sliding or abrasive conditions that mimic real-world wear applications, including specific applied loads, speeds, and contact stresses.
prior_attempts: Previous research has looked into mechanisms like oxidation-induced passivation layers and deformation-induced microstructural evolution (for instance, grain refinement or phase transformations) without isolating a single dominant mechanism.
These multi-mechanism approaches fell short in providing a clear, out-of-baseline controlled experiment that would distinctly confirm one mechanism over the others.

decision.trend: Early research on HEA wear performance moved from multi‐mechanism narratives – where dynamic microstructural evolution (e.g., grain refinement, recrystallization) and oxidation/passivation effects were both observed – toward recognizing that controlled processing can enable one mechanism to dominate. For instance, PMC7515071 demonstrated that under elevated temperatures, wear resistance improved coincident with the formation of a spinel phase, suggesting that in situ oxidation leads to a protective tribolayer. PMC7304825 further showed that processing conditions (e.g., annealing) modified film microstructure and adhesion, which in turn impacted tribological behavior. Despite these advances, experiments have only indirectly probed the roles of transient tribolayer formation versus changes in the microstructure (like grain boundary density) without decisively isolating one mechanism.
decision.unsolved: The dominant mechanistic control over wear performance—whether improved behavior stems primarily from the formation of an oxidation-induced, protective tribolayer that passivates the surface during wear, or from microstructure stabilization (e.g., via enhanced grain boundary densities) that limits deformation—is still ambiguous. In other words, a controlled, out-of-baseline experiment that distinctly links a tuning parameter with enhanced tribolayer formation and improved wear resistance over a given temperature/load range remains to be performed.
decision.lever: Introduce a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment to systematically adjust the coating’s grain boundary density and oxidation kinetics. For example, vary annealing temperature and dwell time to promote or suppress the formation of a continuous tribolayer during simulated sliding wear tests.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend of leveraging microstructural control to impact surface reactions noted in earlier studies. By intentionally modifying the grain boundary density, the treatment should alter the availability of fast diffusion paths for key alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Al) that form the protective oxide. Improved wear performance under expected load/temperature conditions (e.g., up to 900 °C in sliding wear tests) would support the hypothesis that oxidation-driven tribolayer formation governs wear resistance. Conversely, absence of the expected tribolayer or wear improvement would falsify it.
